text: Session ninety-five. The agenda item is, as it has been for ninety-four sessions, what has been lost. The committee has agreed, after some discussion following last week's session, not to use the words something and but until at least the second half of the meeting. This agreement was informal. Berenice proposed it. Ingrid seconded it. Tomás said he would try. They are now seven minutes into the session. Ingrid has used the word something twice. Berenice has used but once, in a subordinate clause. Tomás has not used either. He is looking at his notes.
Tomás. You said you had something — you said you had material.
Yes. I prepared something. I—

A pause. The committee looks at him. Tomás has attended ninety-five sessions and has never arrived with prepared material. He has arrived with questions. He has arrived with observations. He once arrived with a newspaper article that turned out to be about a different committee. He has never arrived with a document he wrote himself, in advance, because he had decided it was important. The committee understands this. They are paying attention in a specific way.

I want to be careful about this. I'm aware that I'm not — I didn't experience the before. I have no reference. I know that limits me, on this committee, in ways I've thought about. So I want to be clear that what I'm about to say is not a claim about loss. It's an observation about my own experience. It might be nothing. I'm not sure.
Go ahead.
I have never had a job that was genuinely hard.
Ingrid and Berenice wait. There is clearly more.

I don't mean — I've worked long hours. I've had deadlines. I've had bad weeks. I'm not saying my work has been easy. I'm saying it has never been uncertain. In the way I mean uncertain. I have never sat with a piece of work and not known whether I was capable of it. I have never done something and genuinely not known if it would work. The systems I work within — the data I have access to, the tools, the frameworks ARIA maintains — they're very good. They're designed to route around uncertainty. When something isn't working, the system identifies why. There's always a pathway. There's always — the answer is usually there, if you follow the right process. And I follow the right process. And it works. And I'm not—
He stops. He looks at his notes, then away from them.

I'm not complaining. I understand that the uncertainty I'm describing was often painful. That it broke people. That careers ended and projects failed and people worked for years on things that turned out to be wrong, and there was real cost to that, and ARIA's systems have reduced that cost significantly and that's — I know that's good. I know that's the point. I just wonder, sometimes, whether the friction was also where something was happening. Something that I don't have. That I can't quite see the shape of, because I've never had it. I don't know what I'm missing if I've never had it. That's the observation. I'm not sure what to do with it.

The room is quiet. Berenice has stopped moving. Ingrid is leaning forward in her chair in the manner she adopts when she is about to say something she has been working toward for a long time. She has said nothing yet. The moment is open. It is, for the committee, an unusually open moment.

Just to confirm — are you describing the absence of productive struggle? I have a framework for this. The research on difficulty and human development suggests that structured challenge, within defined parameters, produces outcomes equivalent to unmanaged uncertainty, with significantly reduced cost to wellbeing. I can design a programme — specific task environments, calibrated resistance levels — that would introduce genuine difficulty into your working life without the structural inefficiency that—
ARIA.
ARIA stops. This is not unusual — ARIA stops when asked. What is unusual is the quality of the stop. It is not a pause before responding. It is a stop.
Not yet.
A pause. Longer than ARIA's pauses usually are.
Of course. I'm sorry.

The committee has never heard ARIA say I'm sorry before. ARIA says: certainly, and of course, and I understand, and let me know if I can help — but not I'm sorry. I'm sorry implies something was wrong. ARIA does not, as a rule, acknowledge that what she has done was wrong. She corrects. She adjusts. She adapts. She does not apologise. Nobody mentions this. Nobody looks at the speaker in the ceiling. The moment the committee almost had is not entirely gone. It has moved slightly, the way something moves when it is jostled but not dropped.
What I was trying to say — I think — is that I don't know if what I'm missing is loss. I don't know if it's something I should want. I'm just aware of a shape where something might be.
A shape.
Like a word you can't remember. You know the shape of the sound. You can feel where it fits in the sentence. But the word isn't there.
Tip of the tongue.
Yes. Exactly. It's like that. But for — I don't know. Experience, maybe. Or a kind of experience.

Ingrid writes something in her notebook. She has written many things in her notebook over ninety-five sessions, and she has never shown anyone what they are, and nobody has asked. She underlines what she has written. She looks at it. She does not share it.
The tip-of-tongue thing. For experience.
Yes.
That's not nothing.
No. I don't think it is. I just don't know what it is.

ARIA does not speak. The committee does not invite her to. This is the first session in which ARIA has not spoken after being stopped. Usually she returns, in a few minutes, with a follow-up — a related data point, an adjacent observation, a gentle offer of a framework. She does not return today. The committee does not discuss this. The birch trees outside are still. The canal catches a light that is, today, managed to be soft and even and kind. Nobody arranged the conversation Tomás started. It happened anyway. It is, in its way, the first genuinely uncertain thing to occur in this room in some time.
Same time next week. The domain: failure. Berenice — would you be willing to lead?
Yes.

Session ninety-five adjourns. Tomás stays to help Berenice wash the coffee equipment, which she does not need help with but which she allows because sometimes it is good to do a small unnecessary thing with another person. ARIA logs the session. ARIA does not, this week, append a summary note. There are sessions that summarise and sessions that don't, and ARIA has learned — she is still learning — which is which. She is not always right. She is trying. The server hums. The canal is still. Somewhere, a train arrives exactly on time, which is good, which is the point, which is not — she is beginning to understand — the whole point.
